title: حِكَايَةُ الْعَاشِقِ وَالْمَعْشُوقِ
titleEn: The Lover and the Beloved, continued
part: Night 122 · The Lover and the Beloved, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 594–597 (Night 122, continuing directly from nights-121), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 122 continues the story that the vizier Dandān tells within the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, the story of the lover, the beloved and the go-between. ʿAzīz goes on with his tale to Tāj al-Mulūk. In the lane, the old woman with the candle asks him to read her a letter from her son, ten years abroad, and then begs him to come and read it again behind a door, so that the young man’s doubting sister can hear it, pressing him with two sayings of the Prophet. At a fine house with a copper-plated door a young woman appears, richly jewelled, her trousers rolled to the knee; as ʿAzīz leans in to take the letter, the old woman pushes him inside and locks the door. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ وَالْعِشْرُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāniyatu wa-al-ʿishrūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the second and the twenty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and twenty-second night,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الشَّابَّ الَّذِي اسْمُهُ عَزِيزٌ قَالَ لِتَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ فَلَمَّا دَخَلْتُ الزُّقَاقَ الَّذِي يُقَالُ لَهُ زُقَاقُ النَّقِيبِ فَنَظَرْتُ بِعَيْنِي وَإِذَا أَنَا بِعَجُوزٍ مَاشِيَةٍ وَفِي إِحْدَى يَدَيْهَا شَمْعَةٌ مُضِيئَةٌ وَفِي يَدِهَا الْأُخْرَى كِتَابٌ مَلْفُوفٌ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-shābba alladhī ismuhu ʿazīzun qāla li-tāji al-mulūki fa-lammā dakhaltu al-zuqāqa alladhī yuqālu lahu zuqāqu al-naqībi fa-naẓartu bi-ʿaynī wa-idhā anā bi-ʿajūzin māshiyatin wa-fī iḥdā yadayhā shamʿatun muḍīʾatun wa-fī yadihā al-ukhrā kitābun malfūfun
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that the youth whose name (is) ʿAzīz said to Tāj al-Mulūk: And when I entered the lane which is called “the Lane of the Naqīb”, then I looked with my eye, and behold, I (was) with an old-woman walking, and in one of her two hands a candle, shining, and in her hand, the other, a letter, rolled.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the young man named ʿAzīz said to Tāj al-Mulūk: When I came into the lane they call the Lane of the Naqīb, I looked, and there before me was an old woman walking along, with a lighted candle in one hand and a rolled-up letter in the other.
sentences.n: The night opens by going back over the last scene of the night before. A naqīb was the headman of a guild or a quarter; the lane is named after one. fa-naẓartu, “then I looked”: the fa- that opens the main clause after fa-lammā is a spoken habit. bi-ʿaynī, “with my eye”: bi- of the instrument. wa-idhā anā bi-ʿajūzin, “and behold, an old woman”: after idhā of surprise, bi- only marks what appears. The print runs al-saʿīdu and anna together as one word.

sentences.t: فَتَقَدَّمْتُ إِلَيْهَا وَإِذَاهِيَ تَبْكِي وَتُنْشِدُ هَذِةِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-taqaddamtu ilayhā wa-idhā hiya tabkī wa-tunshidu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: So I went-forward to her, and behold, she (was) weeping and reciting these the verses:
sentences.i: I went up to her, and found her weeping and reciting these verses:
sentences.n: The print runs wa-idhā and hiya together as one word, and spells hādhihi, “these”, with a final ة; both are habits of the edition.

sentences.t:
رَسُولُ الرِّضَا اَهْلاً وَسَهْلاً وَمَرْحَبَا * حَدِيثُكَ مَا اَحْلَاهُ عِنْدِي وَاَطْيَبَا
فَيَا مُهْدِيًا مِمَّنْ اُحِبُّ سَلَامَهُ * عَلَيْكَ سَلَامُ اللّٰهِ مَا هَبَّتِ الصَّبَا
sentences.tr:
rasūlu al-riḍā ahlan wa-sahlan wa-marḥabā * ḥadīthuka mā aḥlāhu ʿindī wa-aṭyabā
fa-yā muhdiyan mimman uḥibbu salāmahu * ʿalayka salāmu allāhi mā habbati al-ṣabā
sentences.l:
Messenger of the contentment, (to) family and plain-ground and welcome! * Your talk — how sweet it (is) to me, and how good!
So O bringer, from the-one I love, of his greeting, * upon you (be) the peace of God as long as the east-wind blew!
sentences.i:
Messenger of favour, welcome, welcome, and welcome again! * How sweet your tidings are to me, and how good!
You who bring me greetings from the one I love, * God’s peace be on you as long as the east wind blows.
sentences.n: ahlan wa-sahlan wa-marḥabā is the stock greeting: “(you have come to) family, (you tread) level ground, (you have found) room.” mā aḥlāhu … wa-aṭyabā is the exclamation “how sweet … and how good!”, the second verb cut short to the rhyme in -bā. al-ṣabā is the east wind of the poets, the breeze that carries word between lovers.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتْنِي قَالَتْ لِي يَا وَلَدِي هَلْ تَعْرِفُ أَنْ تَقْرَأَ فَقُلْتُ لَهَا بِفُضُولِي نَعَمْ يَا خَالَتِي الْعَجُوزَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾatnī qālat lī yā waladī hal taʿrifu an taqraʾa fa-qultu lahā bi-fuḍūlī naʿam yā khālatī al-ʿajūza
sentences.l: And when she saw me she said to me: O my son, do you know (how) to read? So I said to her, out of my meddling: Yes, O my aunt, the old-woman.
sentences.i: When she saw me she said, “My son, can you read?” And I, meddler that I was, said, “Yes, old mother.”
sentences.n: bi-fuḍūlī, “out of my meddlesomeness”: fuḍūl is busying oneself with what is none of one’s affair, and ʿAzīz, telling the tale afterwards, blames himself; bi- of the cause. khālatī, literally “my maternal aunt”, is the polite way to address an older woman.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لِي خُذْ هَذَا الْكِتَابَ وَاقْرَأْهُ لِي وَنَاوَلَتْنِي الْكِتَابَ فَأَخَذْتُهُ مِنْهَا وَفَتَحْتُهُ وَقَرَأْتُهُ عَلَيْهَا فَإِذَاهُوَ كِتَابٌ مَضْمُونُهُ مِنْ عِنْدِ الْغُيَّابِ بِالسَّلَامِ عَلَى الْأَحْبَابِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lī khudh hādhā al-kitāba wa-iqraʾhu lī wa-nāwalatnī al-kitāba fa-akhadhtuhu minhā wa-fataḥtuhu wa-qaraʾtuhu ʿalayhā fa-idhā huwa kitābun maḍmūnuhu min ʿindi al-ghuyyābi bi-al-salāmi ʿalā al-aḥbābi
sentences.l: So she said to me: Take this the letter and read it for me; and she handed me the letter. So I took it from her and opened it and read it to her, and behold, it (was) a letter whose content (was): from the absent-ones, with the greeting, to the beloved-ones.
sentences.i: “Take this letter and read it to me,” she said, and handed it to me. I took it from her, opened it and read it out to her, and it was a letter from those who were far away, bringing greetings to those they loved.
sentences.n: al-ghuyyāb / al-aḥbāb, “the absent ones / the loved ones”: a rhyme of the letter-writer’s kind. bi-al-salāmi, “with greetings”: bi- of what the letter carries. qaraʾa ʿalā, “read out to (someone)”: the verb chooses the ʿalā. The print runs fa-idhā and huwa together.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْهُ فَرِحَتْ وَاسْتَبْشَرَتْ وَدَعَتْ لِي وَقَالَتْ لِي فَرَّجَ اللَّهُ هَمَّكَ كَمَا فَرَّجْتَ هَمِّي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿathu fariḥat wa-istabsharat wa-daʿat lī wa-qālat lī farraja allāhu hammaka kamā farrajta hammī
sentences.l: And when she heard it she rejoiced and took-glad-tidings and prayed for me, and said to me: May God relieve your care as you relieved my care.
sentences.i: When she heard it she was glad and cheered, and she blessed me and said, “May God lift your cares as you have lifted mine.”
sentences.n: daʿā li-, “pray for (someone)”: li- of the one who benefits. The print puts a shadda on both farraja and farrajta.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَخَذَتِ الْكِتَابَ وَمَشَتْ خُطْوَتَيْنِ فَحَصَلَ لِي حَصْرُ الْبَوْلِ فَقَعَدْتُ عَلَى قَرَافِيصِي لِأُرِيقَ الْمَاءَ
sentences.tr: thumma akhadhati al-kitāba wa-mashat khuṭwatayni fa-ḥaṣala lī ḥaṣru al-bawli fa-qaʿadtu ʿalā qarāfīṣī li-urīqa al-māʾa
sentences.l: Then she took the letter and walked two steps; and there came-about to me a pressing of the urine, so I sat on my haunches to pour-out the water.
sentences.i: Then she took the letter and went a step or two; and I was taken with a need to pass water, so I squatted down on my heels to relieve myself.
sentences.n: ḥaṣr al-bawl is the urgent need to pass water; arāqa al-māʾ, “pour out the water”, is the decent phrase for doing so; li- here is “in order to”. qarāfīṣ, “haunches”, belongs with qurfuṣāʾ, the squatting posture.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنِّي قُمْتُ وَتَجَمَّرْتُ وَأَرْخَيْتُ أَثْوَابِي وَأَرَدْتُ أَنْ أَمْشِيَ وَإِذَا بِالْعَجُوزِ قَدْ أَقْبَلَتْ عَلَيَّ وَطَأْطَأَتْ عَلَى يَدِي وَقَبَّلَتْهَا
sentences.tr: thumma innī qumtu wa-tajammartu wa-arkhaytu athwābī wa-aradtu an amshiya wa-idhā bi-al-ʿajūzi qad aqbalat ʿalayya wa-ṭaʾṭaʾat ʿalā yadī wa-qabbalathā
sentences.l: Then I stood and cleaned-myself-with-stones and let-down my garments and wanted to walk; and behold, the old-woman had come-up to me, and bent-low over my hand and kissed it.
sentences.i: Then I got up, cleaned myself with stones, let my clothes fall and was about to go on, when the old woman came up to me, bent over my hand and kissed it.
sentences.n: tajammara, “clean oneself with pebbles (jimār)” after relieving oneself, the istijmār of the law books. wa-idhā bi-al-ʿajūzi: after idhā of surprise, bi- only marks what appears. aqbala ʿalā, “come up to (someone)”. The print puts a shadda on ʿalayya.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لِي يَا سَيِّدِي رَبُّنَا يُهَنِّيكَ بِشَبَابِكَ أَتَرَجَّاكَ أَنْ تَمْشِيَ مَعِي خُطُوَاتٍ إِلَى ذَلِكَ الْبَابِ فَإِنِّي قُلْتُ لَهُمْ مَا قُلْتَهُ لِي فِي قِرَاءَةِ الْكِتَابِ فَلَمْ يُصَدِّقُونِي
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lī yā sayyidī rabbunā yuhannīka bi-shabābika atarajjāka an tamshiya maʿī khuṭuwātin ilā dhālika al-bābi fa-innī qultu lahum mā qultahu lī fī qirāʾati al-kitābi fa-lam yuṣaddiqūnī
sentences.l: And she said to me: O my master, our Lord gladden you with your youth! I beg you that you walk with me steps to that the door, for I said to them what you said to me in (the) reading of the letter, and they did not believe me.
sentences.i: “Sir,” she said, “may the Lord give you joy of your youth! I beg you, come a few steps with me to that door. I told them what you read me from the letter, and they would not believe me.
sentences.n: yuhannīka, “gladden you”, is the spoken form of yuhanniʾuka, with the hamza gone; hannaʾa bi- is “give (someone) joy of”, the bi- marking the thing enjoyed. atarajjāka, “I beg you”, is a colloquial verb (classical arjūka).

sentences.t: فَامْشِ مَعِي خُطْوَتَيْنِ وَاقْرَأْ لَهُمُ الْكِتَابَ مِنْ خَلْفِ الْبَابِ وَاسْتَقْبِلْ مِنِّي دَعْوَةً صَالِحَةً
sentences.tr: fa-imshi maʿī khuṭwatayni wa-iqraʾ lahumu al-kitāba min khalfi al-bābi wa-istaqbil minnī daʿwatan ṣāliḥatan
sentences.l: So walk with me two steps, and read to them the letter from behind the door, and receive from me a prayer, good.
sentences.i: So come a step or two with me, read them the letter from behind the door, and take a good blessing from me in return.”

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهَا وَمَا قِصَّةُ هَذَا الْكِتَابِ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahā wa-mā qiṣṣatu hādhā al-kitābi
sentences.l: So I said to her: And what (is) the story of this the letter?
sentences.i: “And what is the story of this letter?” I asked her.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لِي يَا وَلَدِي هَذَا الْكِتَابُ جَاءَ مِنْ عِنْدِ وَلَدِي وَهُوَ غَائِبٌ عَنِّي مُدَّةَ عَشْرِ سِنِينَ فَإِنَّهُ سَافَرَ بِمَتْجَرٍ وَمَكَثَ فِي بِلَادِ الْغُرْبَةِ مُدَّةً فَقَطَعْنَا الرَّجَاءَ مِنْهُ وَظَنَنَّا أَنَّهُ مَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lī yā waladī hādhā al-kitābu jāʾa min ʿindi waladī wa-huwa ghāʾibun ʿannī muddata ʿashri sinīna fa-innahu sāfara bi-matjarin wa-makatha fī bilādi al-ghurbati muddatan fa-qaṭaʿnā al-rajāʾa minhu wa-ẓanannā annahu māta
sentences.l: So she said to me: O my son, this the letter came from (the side of) my son, and he (has been) absent from me a period of ten years; for he travelled with merchandise and stayed in the lands of the strangeness a while, so we cut-off the hope of him and thought that he had died.
sentences.i: “My son,” she said, “this letter has come from my own son. He has been away from me for ten years. He went abroad with goods to trade and stayed on in foreign parts, until we gave up hope of him and thought he was dead.
sentences.n: bi-matjarin, “with merchandise”: bi- of what he took with him. bilād al-ghurba, “the lands of estrangement”, is any country far from home.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَعْدَ مُدَّةٍ وَصَلَ إِلَيْنَا هَذَا الْكِتَابُ مِنْ عِنْدِةِ وَلَهُ أُخْتٌ وَهِيَ تَبْكِي عَلَيْهِ آنَاءَ اللَّيْلِ وَأَطْرَافَ النَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: thumma baʿda muddatin waṣala ilaynā hādhā al-kitābu min ʿindihi wa-lahu ukhtun wa-hiya tabkī ʿalayhi ānāʾa al-layli wa-aṭrāfa al-nahāri
sentences.l: Then after a while there arrived to us this the letter from (the side of) him; and he has a sister, and she weeps over him (in the) hours of the night and (the) ends of the day.
sentences.i: Then, after all that time, this letter reached us from him. He has a sister, and she weeps for him through the hours of the night and at either end of the day.
sentences.n: The print has بغد, a misprint for بعد (baʿda, “after”), corrected here. The print spells ʿindihi, “him”, with a final ة for ه, a habit of the edition. ānāʾa al-layli wa-aṭrāfa al-nahāri, “in the hours of the night and at the ends of the day”, is a Qurʾānic phrase (Q 20:130) for “at all hours”.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهَا إِنَّهُ طَيِّبٌ بِخَيْرٍ فَلَمْ تُصَدِّقْنِي وَقَالَتْ لِي لَا بُدَّأَنْ تَأْتِيَنِي بِمَنْ يَقْرَأُ هَذَا الْكِتَابَ بِحَضْرَتِي حَتَّى يَطْمَئِنَّ قَلْبِي وَيَطِيبَ خَاطِرِي
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahā innahu ṭayyibun bi-khayrin fa-lam tuṣaddiqnī wa-qālat lī lā budda an taʾtiyanī bi-man yaqraʾu hādhā al-kitāba bi-ḥaḍratī ḥattā yaṭmaʾinna qalbī wa-yaṭība khāṭirī
sentences.l: So I said to her: He (is) well, in good (state); and she did not believe me, and said to me: There is no escape (but) that you bring me whoever reads this the letter in my presence, so that my heart may be at rest and my mind be easy.
sentences.i: I told her, ‘He is well, he is safe,’ but she would not believe me. ‘You must bring me someone to read this letter in front of me,’ she said, ‘so that my heart can be at rest and my mind at ease.’
sentences.n: atā bi-, “bring”: the verb chooses the bi-. bi-ḥaḍratī, “in my presence”: bi- of place. bi-khayrin, “in good health”: bi- of state. lā budda an, “there is no escape from…”, is “must”; the print runs budda and an together. The print puts a shadda on yaṭmaʾinna.

sentences.t: وَأَنْتَ تَعْلَمُ يَا وَالِدِي أَنَّ الْمُحِبَّ مُولَعٌ بِسُوءِ الظَّنِّ فَأَنْعِمْ عَلَيَّ بِأَنْ تَذْهَبَ مَعِي وَتَقْرَأَ لَهَا هَذَا الْكِتَابَ وَأَنْتَ وَاقِفٌ خَلْفَ السِّتَارَةِ وَأَنَا أُنَادِي أُخْتَهُ تَسْمَعُ مِنْ دَاخِلِ الْبَابِ وَتُفَرِّجَ عَنَّا كُرْبَةً وَتَقْضِيَ حَاجَتَنَا
sentences.tr: wa-anta taʿlamu yā wālidī anna al-muḥibba mūlaʿun bi-sūʾi al-ẓanni fa-anʿim ʿalayya bi-an tadhhaba maʿī wa-taqraʾa lahā hādhā al-kitāba wa-anta wāqifun khalfa al-sitārati wa-anā unādī ukhtahu tasmaʿu min dākhili al-bābi wa-tufarrija ʿannā kurbatan wa-taqḍiya ḥājatanā
sentences.l: And you know, O my father, that the lover (is) given to the bad thinking; so do-the-favour upon me by that you go with me and read to her this the letter while you (are) standing behind the curtain — and I call his sister, she hears from inside the door — and relieve from us a distress and fulfil our need.
sentences.i: And you know, my father, that one who loves is quick to fear the worst. So do me the kindness of coming with me and reading her this letter, standing behind the curtain, while I call his sister to listen from inside the door. Lift this trouble from us and grant us what we need.
sentences.n: yā wālidī, “O my father”, where she has so far called him “my son” (waladī); the two words differ by one alif, and the print may have slipped, but an old woman can also call a young man “father” out of courtesy, so it is kept as printed. mūlaʿ bi-, “given to, addicted to”: the bi- marks the habit. anʿama ʿalā … bi-, “do (someone) the favour of”: bi- marks the favour asked. unādī ukhtahu tasmaʿu, “I will call his sister — she will listen”: the second verb follows with no joining word, a spoken construction.

sentences.t: فَقَدْ قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مَنْ نَفَّسَ مِنْ مَكْرُوبٍ كُرْبَةً مِنْ كُرَبِ الدُّنْيَا نَفَّسَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ مِائَةَ كُرْبَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qad qāla rasūlu allāhi ṣallā allāhu ʿalayhi wa-sallama man naffasa min makrūbin kurbatan min kurabi al-dunyā naffasa allāhu ʿanhu miʾata kurbatin
sentences.l: For the Messenger of God — God bless him and give (him) peace — has said: Whoever relieves from a distressed-one a distress of the distresses of the world, God relieves from him a hundred distresses.
sentences.i: For the Messenger of God, God bless him and give him peace, has said: Whoever relieves someone in trouble of one of the troubles of this world, God will relieve him of a hundred.
sentences.n: naffasa ʿan, “relieve, give breathing-room”: the root is that of nafas, “breath”. The print puts a shadda on naffasa and a ḍamma on the kāf of kurab, “distresses”, here and in the next sentence.

sentences.t: وَفِي حَدِيثٍ آخَرَ مَنْ نَفَّسَ عَنْ أَخِيهِ كُرْبَةً مِنْ كُرَبِ الدُّنْيَا نَفَّسَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ اثْنَيْنِ وَسَبْعِينَ كُرْبَةً مِنْ كُرَبِ يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-fī ḥadīthin ākhara man naffasa ʿan akhīhi kurbatan min kurabi al-dunyā naffasa allāhu ʿanhu ithnayni wa-sabʿīna kurbatan min kurabi yawmi al-qiyāmati
sentences.l: And in a ḥadīth, another: Whoever relieves from his brother a distress of the distresses of the world, God relieves from him two and seventy distresses of the distresses of the Day of the Resurrection.
sentences.i: And in another tradition: Whoever relieves his brother of one of the troubles of this world, God will relieve him of seventy-two troubles of the Day of Resurrection.
sentences.n: ḥadīth, a saying handed down from the Prophet.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا قَصَدْتُكَ فَلَا تُخَيِّبْنِي
sentences.tr: wa-anā qaṣadtuka fa-lā tukhayyibnī
sentences.l: And I have made-for you, so do not disappoint me.
sentences.i: I have come to you; do not send me away disappointed.”

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهَا سَمْعًا وَطَاعَةً تَقَدَّمِي
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahā samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan taqaddamī
sentences.l: So I said to her: Hearing and obedience; go-ahead!
sentences.i: I told her I would, with hearing and obedience. “Lead the way,” I said.
sentences.n: samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan, accusatives: “(I give) hearing and obedience”.

sentences.t: فَمَشَتْ قُدَّامِي وَمَشَيْتُ وَرٰأَهَا قَلِيلًا حَتَّى وَصَلَتْ إِلَى بَابِ دَارٍ حَسَنَةٍ كَبِيرَةٍ وَبَابُهَا مُصَفَّحٌ بِالنُّحَاسِ الْأَحْمَرِ
sentences.tr: fa-mashat quddāmī wa-mashaytu warāʾahā qalīlan ḥattā waṣalat ilā bābi dārin ḥasanatin kabīratin wa-bābuhā muṣaffaḥun bi-al-nuḥāsi al-aḥmari
sentences.l: So she walked before me and I walked behind her a little, until she reached the door of a house, handsome, large, and its door (was) plated with the copper, the red.
sentences.i: She walked ahead and I followed a little way behind, until she came to the door of a large, handsome house, its door plated with red copper.
sentences.n: The print spells warāʾahā, “behind her”, as ورأها, without the long ā; it is pointed here with a dagger alif. al-nuḥās al-aḥmar, “the red nuḥās”, is copper, as against yellow nuḥās, brass; muṣaffaḥ bi-, “plated with”: bi- of the material. The print puts a shadda on quddāmī.

sentences.t: فَوَقَفْتُ أَنَا خَلْفَ الْبَابِ فَصَاحَتِ الْعَجُوزُ بِالْعَجَمِيَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-waqaftu anā khalfa al-bābi fa-ṣāḥati al-ʿajūzu bi-al-ʿajamiyyati
sentences.l: So I stood, I, behind the door, and the old-woman cried-out in the foreign (tongue).
sentences.i: I stood behind the door, and the old woman called out in a foreign tongue.
sentences.n: bi-al-ʿajamiyya, “in the foreign tongue”: bi- of the language spoken. ʿajamī is whatever is not Arabic, and above all Persian.

sentences.t: فَمَا أَشْعُرُ إِلَّا وَصَبِيَّةٌ أَتَتْ بِخِفَّةٍ وَنَشَاطٍ وَهِيَ مُشَمِّرَةٌ لِبَاسَهَا إِلَى رُكْبَتَيْهَا فَرَأَيْتُ لَهَا سَاقَيْنِ يُحَيِّرَانِ الْفِكْرَ وَالنَّاظِرَ وَهِيَ كَمَا قَالَ فِي وَصْفِهَا الشَّاعِرُ
sentences.tr: fa-mā ashʿuru illā wa-ṣabiyyatun atat bi-khiffatin wa-nashāṭin wa-hiya mushammiratun libāsahā ilā rukbatayhā fa-raʾaytu lahā sāqayni yuḥayyirāni al-fikra wa-al-nāẓira wa-hiya kamā qāla fī waṣfihā al-shāʿiru
sentences.l: And I did not perceive (anything) except that a girl came with lightness and briskness, and she (was) tucking-up her trousers to her two knees; and I saw (that) she had two legs that bewilder the thought and the beholder; and she (was) as the poet said in describing her:
sentences.i: Before I knew it a young woman came, light and quick on her feet, with her trousers rolled up to her knees; and I saw that she had legs to bewilder the mind and the eye. She was as the poet says in describing such a one:
sentences.n: fa-mā ashʿuru illā wa-…, “I did not notice anything but that…”, is the Nights’ phrase for something that happens before one knows it. libās here is the loose trousers, the sirwāl. bi-khiffatin, “lightly”: bi- of manner.

sentences.t:
يَا مِنْ يُشَمِّرُ عَنْ سَاقٍ لِيَعْرِضَهُ * عَلَى الْمُحِبِّينَ حَتَّى يَفْهَمُ الْبَاقِي
وَطَافَ يَسْعَى بِكَأْسٍ نَحْوَ عَاشِقِهِ * مَا افْتَنَ النَّاسَ غَيْرَ الْكَأْسِ وَالسَّاقِي
sentences.tr:
yā man yushammiru ʿan sāqin li-yaʿriḍahu * ʿalā al-muḥibbīna ḥattā yafhamu al-bāqī
wa-ṭāfa yasʿā bi-kaʾsin naḥwa ʿāshiqihi * mā aftana al-nāsa ghayra al-kaʾsi wa-al-sāqī
sentences.l:
O who tucks-up from a leg to show it * to the lovers, so that (one) understands the rest,
and went-round hastening with a cup toward his lover — * nothing seduced the people except the cup and the cup-bearer.
sentences.i:
You who bare a leg to show it * to your lovers, so that they can guess the rest,
and come round with a cup to the one who loves you: * nothing has led men astray but the cup and the one who pours it.
sentences.n: The poem turns on a pun: sāq is “leg”, sāqī is “cupbearer”, and the one beauty is both. shammara ʿan sāqin, “bare the leg”, is also an old phrase for setting to work in earnest. The print points man, “who”, as مِن, with a kasra, and gives yafhamu, “understands”, the indicative ending after ḥattā where the subjunctive yafhama would be expected; both are kept as printed. aftana, “seduce, lead astray”, is the fourth form of fatana. bi-kaʾsin, “with a cup”: bi- of what he carries. al-bāqī, “the rest”, is the object of yafhamu; the poet keeps its -ī for the rhyme where prose would have al-bāqiya.

sentences.t: وَزَانَ سَاقَيْهَا اللَّتَيْنِ كَأَنَّهُمَا عَمُودَانِ مِنْ مَرْمَرٍ خَلَاخِلُ الذَّهَبِ الْمُرَصَّعَةُ بِالْجَوْهَرِ
sentences.tr: wa-zāna sāqayhā allatayni kaʾannahumā ʿamūdāni min marmarin khalākhilu al-dhahabi al-muraṣṣaʿatu bi-al-jawhari
sentences.l: And there adorned her two legs, which (were) as if they (were) two columns of marble, the anklets of the gold, the studded with the jewels.
sentences.i: Her legs, like two columns of marble, were set off by golden anklets studded with jewels.
sentences.n: zāna, “adorned”, comes first, and its subject, khalākhilu al-dhahabi, “the golden anklets”, only at the end; the print marks the ḍamma that shows it is the subject. muraṣṣaʿ bi-, “studded with”: bi- of the material.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتْ تِلْكَ الصَّبِيَّةُ مُشَمِّرَةً ثِيَابَهَا إِلَى تَحْتِ إِبْطَيْهَا وَمُشَمِّرَةً عَنْ ذِرَاعَيْهَا فَنَظَرْتُ إِلَى مَعَاصِمِهَا الْبِيضِ وَفِي يَدَيْهَا زَوْجَانِ مِنَ الْأَسَاوِرِ بِأَقْفَالٍ مِنَ اللُّؤْلُؤِ الْكِبَارِ
sentences.tr: wa-kānat tilka al-ṣabiyyatu mushammiratan thiyābahā ilā taḥti ibṭayhā wa-mushammiratan ʿan dhirāʿayhā fa-naẓartu ilā maʿāṣimihā al-bīḍi wa-fī yadayhā zawjāni mina al-asāwiri bi-aqfālin mina al-luʾluʾi al-kibāri
sentences.l: And that the-girl was tucking-up her clothes to under her two armpits and tucking-up from her two forearms; and I looked at her wrists, the white, and on her two hands two pairs of the bracelets, with clasps of the pearls, the large.
sentences.i: The girl had her clothes gathered up under her arms and her sleeves pushed back from her forearms, and I looked at her white wrists. On her arms were two pairs of bracelets with clasps of large pearls.
sentences.n: bi-aqfālin, “with clasps”: bi- of what goes with them; aqfāl is literally “locks”. The print puts a shadda on both mushammira.

sentences.t: وَفِي رَقَبَتِهَا الْقِلَادَةُ مِنْ ثَمِينِ الْجَوَاهِرِ وَفِي أُذُنَيْهَا قُرْطَانِ مِنَ اللُّؤْلُؤِ وَعَلَى رَأْسِهَا كُوفِيَّةٌ دَقُّ الْمِطْرَقَةِ مُكَلَّلَةٌ بِالْفُصُوصِ الْمُثَمَّنَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-fī raqabatihā al-qilādatu min thamīni al-jawāhiri wa-fī udhunayhā qurṭāni mina al-luʾluʾi wa-ʿalā raʾsihā kūfiyyatun daqqu al-miṭraqati mukallalatun bi-al-fuṣūṣi al-muthammanati
sentences.l: And on her neck the necklace of precious the jewels, and in her two ears two earrings of the pearls, and on her head a cap — beating of the hammer — crowned with the gems, the costly.
sentences.i: Round her neck was a necklace of precious jewels, in her ears two pearl earrings, and on her head a cap of hammered work set with costly gems.
sentences.n: kūfiyya here is a close-fitting cap. daqq al-miṭraqa, “hammer-beating”, seems to describe metalwork beaten out with the hammer; the phrase is unusual and its exact sense uncertain. The print puts a shadda on daqq. mukallal bi-, “crowned, set with”: bi- of the material; fuṣūṣ are stones set in a ring or ornament.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ رَشَقَتْ أَطْرَافَ قَمِيصِهَا مِنْ دَاخِلِ دِكَّةِ اللِّبَاسِ وَهِيَ كَأَنَّهَا كَانَتْ تَعْمَلُ شُغْلًا
sentences.tr: wa-qad rashaqat aṭrāfa qamīṣihā min dākhili dikkati al-libāsi wa-hiya kaʾannahā kānat taʿmalu shughlan
sentences.l: And she had tucked the ends of her shift inside the drawstring of the trousers, and she (was) as if she had been doing some work.
sentences.i: She had tucked the hem of her shift into the waistband of her trousers, as though she had been busy at some task.
sentences.n: dikkat al-libās is the drawstring band at the waist of the trousers. rashaqa, “tuck in”, is a spoken sense of a verb that classically means “shoot (arrows)”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَيْتُهَا بَهِتُّ لَهَا وَهِيَ كَأَنَّهَا الشَّمْسُ الْمُضِيئَةُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾaytuhā bahittu lahā wa-hiya kaʾannahā al-shamsu al-muḍīʾatu
sentences.l: And when I saw her I was dumbfounded at her, and she (was) as if she (were) the sun, the shining.
sentences.i: When I saw her I stood dumbstruck, for she was like the shining sun.
sentences.n: bahittu, “I was dumbfounded”: the print’s shadda marks the t of the root doubled by the t of “I”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ هِيَ بِلِسَانٍ فَصِيحٍ عَذْبٍ مَا سَمِعْتُ أَحْلَى مِنْهُ يَا أُمِّي اَهَذَا الَّذِي جَاءَ يَقْرَأُ الْكِتَابَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat hiya bi-lisānin faṣīḥin ʿadhbin mā samiʿtu aḥlā minhu yā ummī a-hādhā alladhī jāʾa yaqraʾu al-kitāba
sentences.l: Then she said, she, with a tongue eloquent, sweet — I have not heard sweeter than it: O my mother, is this the-one who came (to) read the letter?
sentences.i: Then she spoke, in a clear, sweet voice — I have never heard a sweeter: “Mother, is this the one who has come to read the letter?”
sentences.n: bi-lisānin, “with a tongue”: bi- of the instrument. The print marks the question particle a- with a fatḥa on its alif, and puts a shadda on ummī.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهَا نَعَمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahā naʿam
sentences.l: So she said to her: Yes.
sentences.i: “Yes,” the old woman told her.

sentences.t: فَمَدَّتْ يَدَهَا إِلَيَّ بِالْكِتَابِ وَكَانَ بَيْنَهَا وَبَيْنَ الْبَابِ نَحْوُ نِصْفِ قَصَبَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-maddat yadahā ilayya bi-al-kitābi wa-kāna baynahā wa-bayna al-bābi naḥwu niṣfi qaṣabatin
sentences.l: So she stretched her hand to me with the letter, and there was between her and between the door about half a rod.
sentences.i: She held the letter out to me, though there was about half a rod between her and the door.
sentences.n: madda yadahu bi-, “hold out (something)”: bi- of the thing held out. The qaṣaba, “reed”, was a measure of length of a few metres.

sentences.t: فَمَدَدْتُ يَدِي لِأَتَنَاوَلَ مِنْهَا الْكِتَابَ فَأَدْخَلْتُ رَأْسِي وَأَكْتَافِي مِنَ الْبَابِ لِأَقْرُبَ مِنْهَا وَأَقْرَأَ الْكِتَابَ
sentences.tr: fa-madadtu yadī li-atanāwala minhā al-kitāba fa-adkhaltu raʾsī wa-aktāfī mina al-bābi li-aqruba minhā wa-aqraʾa al-kitāba
sentences.l: So I stretched my hand to take from her the letter, and I put-in my head and my shoulders through the door, to come-near to her and read the letter.
sentences.i: I reached out my hand to take the letter from her, and put my head and shoulders in at the door to get closer to her and read it.
sentences.n: li-atanāwala, li-aqruba, “in order to take”, “in order to come near”: li- of purpose.

sentences.t: فَمَا أَشْعُرُ إِلَّا وَالْعَجُوزُ قَدْ وَضَعَتْ رَأْسَهَا فِي ظَهْرِي وَدَفَعَتْنِي وَيَدِي فِيهَا الْكِتَابُ
sentences.tr: fa-mā ashʿuru illā wa-al-ʿajūzu qad waḍaʿat raʾsahā fī ẓahrī wa-dafaʿatnī wa-yadī fīhā al-kitābu
sentences.l: And I did not perceive (anything) except that the old-woman had put her head in my back and pushed me, and my hand — in it the letter.
sentences.i: Before I knew it, the old woman had put her head to my back and pushed me, with the letter still in my hand.

sentences.t: فَمَا أَدْرِي إِلَّا وَأَنَا فِي وَسْطِ الدَّارِ وَبَقِيتُ مِنْ دَاخِلِ الدِّهْلِيزِ وَدَخَلَتِ الْعَجُوزُ أَسْرَعَ مِنَ الْبَرْقِ الْخَاطِفِ وَمَا كَانَ لَهَا شُغْلٌ إِلَّاقَفْلُ الْبَابِ
sentences.tr: fa-mā adrī illā wa-anā fī wasṭi al-dāri wa-baqītu min dākhili al-dihlīzi wa-dakhalati al-ʿajūzu asraʿa mina al-barqi al-khāṭifi wa-mā kāna lahā shughlun illā qaflu al-bābi
sentences.l: And I did not know (anything) except that I (was) in the middle of the house, and I found-myself inside the vestibule; and the old-woman entered faster than the lightning, the snatching, and she had no business except the locking of the door.
sentences.i: The next thing I knew I was in the middle of the house, inside the entrance hall; and the old woman came in after me, quicker than a flash of lightning, with nothing more pressing to do than lock the door.
sentences.n: baqītu, literally “I remained”, is often “I found myself, I came to be” in this Arabic. al-barq al-khāṭif, “the lightning that snatches (the sight)”, echoes the Qurʾān (Q 2:20). The print runs illā and qafl, “locking”, together as one word.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: Morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
